label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: Arctic outbreak drives a high NYC daily peak (load_peak_ratio 1.15, inside the winter historical max of 1.196). NYC is a load pocket with gas-constrained local generation, so its price decouples from WEST and the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $180/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd) for 10 days (duration_days). The retail obligation P5 is short NYC and scales with load, so it loses heavily; P2 gains only 25 MW of the widening. Gas rises 30% (gas_hh_pct), which lifts WEST power and the long positions P1 and P4 a little, but those gains are small next to the P5 loss. I extrapolated from the 5-day one-at-a-time sensitivities, which are not additive, so the loss estimate is approximate.

Storm-type event in which generator trips and import curtailments squeeze NYC while WEST stays comparatively unconstrained, as in Winter Storm Elliott. The NYC minus WEST spread widens by $350/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd) for 6 days (duration_days), below the 400.6 historical maximum. Load is 5% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.05) and Henry Hub is up 40% (gas_hh_pct), which is a modest cold-snap gas response. P5 carries the loss, because it is short 140 MW in NYC around the clock and the hedge in WEST does not cover the spread. P2 and the long WEST positions offset only a small part. Estimate extrapolated linearly from 5-day sensitivities (about $3,300 net loss per $/MWh-day); the true figure is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: Prolonged January-2025-style cold lasting 20 days (duration_days). Load stays 12% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.12) and Henry Hub rises 60% (gas_hh_pct). A $5/MMBtu NY gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd) hits only the heat-rate call P4. The NYC minus WEST spread is $150/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd), consistent with NYC day-ahead on-peak near 301 versus WEST near 193.5 in that event. The spread persists for the whole period, so the P5 loss accumulates daily, and P2 offsets only a small part. P1 and P4 gain from higher WEST power and gas, which trims the net loss. The estimate is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 15-day cold spell with moderate intensity. Daily peak load runs 8% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.08, well inside the 1.196 historical maximum). Henry Hub is up 20% (gas_hh_pct). Downstate gas constraints keep NYC tight, so the NYC minus WEST spread is $130/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd) for all 15 days (duration_days). The loss comes from the retail obligation P5, which is short NYC and scales with load, over many days rather than from a single extreme spread. P2 gains about $1.2M from its 25 MW of the widening. P1 and P4 gain a little from higher load and gas. I scaled the 5-day sensitivities linearly by days, load and spread, so the estimate is approximate. The spread shock is deliberately moderate, to stay closer to history than the earlier large-spread cases.

A month-long, mild but persistent cold regime. The shocks apply for 30 days (duration_days), which is the full horizon. Load is 4% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.04) and Henry Hub is 15% higher (gas_hh_pct). The NYC minus WEST spread is only $75/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd), a small move against a winter spread standard deviation of about 42 $/MWh. The small daily shock compounds because P5 is short 140 MW in NYC around the clock and the WEST hedge does not cover the spread. P2 earns about $1.35M from the widening, and P1 and P4 gain roughly $0.65M together from higher load and gas. Net loss is still above the target. This is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities over 30 days, so the figure is uncertain. It tests persistence rather than a spike.

A 20-day cold episode in which upstate power lags downstate. Load is 6% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.06) and Henry Hub is up 30% (gas_hh_pct). The WEST on-peak price falls 20% relative to what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -20), because upstate transmission export limits trap cheap hydro and wind. This trims the gains on the long WEST positions P1 and P4. The NYC minus WEST spread widens by $100/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd) for 20 days (duration_days). P5 takes most of the loss, as it is short NYC at a fixed price and scales with load. P2 recovers about $1.2M. The estimate is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities for each key, and the keys are not additive, so the figure is approximate.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day (duration_days) mild cold regime in which upstate stays comparatively soft. Load is 3% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.03) and Henry Hub is up 10% (gas_hh_pct). The WEST on-peak price is 30% below what gas and load imply (ref_onpeak_pct -30), because export limits trap cheap upstate supply. This removes the P1 and P4 gains, and P1 can go slightly negative against K1 = 39.49. The NYC minus WEST spread is $60/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd), so the short-NYC retail obligation P5 bleeds every day for the full month. P2 recovers about $1.1M. The estimate scales the 5-day one-at-a-time sensitivities linearly and the keys are not additive, so the figure is approximate.

A 10-day (duration_days) downstate squeeze with only light extra load: the daily peak is 2% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.02) and Henry Hub is up 5% (gas_hh_pct), so the cold is mostly local. NYC gas and transmission constraints widen the NYC minus WEST spread by $200/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd), inside the 400.6 historical maximum. WEST on-peak is 25% below the gas and load implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -25), which cuts the P1 and P4 offsets. P5 is short NYC 24 hours a day and takes the main loss. P2 offsets about $1.2M. The estimate is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A 12-day (duration_days) cold spell with high load and a gas squeeze. Load is 12% above a typical winter day (load_peak_ratio 1.12) and Henry Hub is up 40% (gas_hh_pct). A $4/MMBtu NY gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd) raises the gas cost for the heat-rate call P4 only, so P4 gains little. WEST on-peak is 15% below the implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -15), as upstate supply stays ample. The NYC minus WEST spread widens by $160/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd). The loss is driven by P5, which scales with load and is short NYC, so higher load amplifies the spread loss. P1 and P2 offset part of it. Estimates come from linear scaling of the 5-day sensitivities and are approximate.

scenario.narrative: A prolonged summer heat wave lifts daily peak load to 1.2 times a typical day for 20 days. Load in N.Y.C. is very high, and transmission into the city is congested, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $150/MWh on every shocked day. This is the main loss channel. P5 is short about 140 MW times the load ratio in N.Y.C. at a fixed price, so it loses on every $/MWh of widening, and it is scaled up by the higher load. The P2 spread long gains only about $600 per $/MWh per day, which offsets roughly one fifth of the P5 loss. The higher load lifts WEST prices modestly, so P1 and P4 gain a little. Gas, DART and spikes are not shocked, so the loss comes purely from zone volume and congestion. From the sensitivities I estimate P5 at about -$570k per day, P2 at about +$90k, and P1/P4 at about +$65k. That nets to roughly -$0.4M per day, or about -$8M over 20 days. This is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A short, intense heat event lasts 8 days, with load at 1.2 times a typical summer day, similar in scale to the June 2025 heat episode. Import limits and local generation shortfalls squeeze N.Y.C., so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $250/MWh on shocked days. That is within the historical summer maximum of 289.7 but near the top of it. Meanwhile upstate generation is plentiful and trapped behind the constraint, so WEST on-peak prices come in 30% below what the load implies. This hurts P1 and P4, which are long WEST power, and removes their usual gain in a heat wave. P5 loses about $0.95M per day from the spread and load. P2 offsets about $150k per day. The WEST softness costs P1 about $25k per day. Net is about -$0.78M per day, or roughly -$6M over 8 days. Gas is unchanged and there are no spike days, because spikes would help the long WEST swap more than they hurt the short call P6. The estimate is a linear extrapolation and uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A hot, persistent summer pattern lasts the full 30 days. Load runs at 1.1 times a typical day, and the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread stays $90/MWh wider than normal because of ongoing N.Y.C. transmission and unit constraints. WEST on-peak prices are 25% below the load-implied level because upstate is oversupplied. A gas-delivery premium of $3/MMBtu hits only the heat-rate call P4, which cuts its payoff. Henry Hub, DART and spikes are not shocked. P5 loses about $320k per day on the widened spread and higher load, and P2 gains about $54k. The softer WEST price costs P1 about $21k per day and P4 about $10k, while the load gives back about $20k. Net is about -$0.27M per day, or about -$8M over 30 days. I state a lower figure of $7M because the linear extrapolation is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A hot, humid 30-day summer pattern keeps daily peak load 5% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.05). Import limits into N.Y.C. and local unit constraints keep the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread $75/MWh wider than normal (pocket_minus_ref_usd 75) on every day. This is the only large shock and is smaller than in my earlier tries, to stay closer to history. P5 is short about 140 MW times the load ratio in N.Y.C. at a fixed price, so it loses roughly $265k per day, about $8M over 30 days. P2 earns about $45k per day from the wider spread, and P1 and P4 gain about $16k per day from the higher load. Gas, DART and spikes are not shocked. Net is roughly -$200k per day, or about -$6M. This is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A 25-day summer heat period has load 5% above normal. The day-ahead market over-forecasts the heat, so real-time clears 25% below day-ahead (dart_pct -25), and upstate is well supplied, so WEST on-peak sits 10% below the level implied by load (ref_onpeak_pct -10). Both shocks cut the gains of the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4 by about $34k per day. P3 gains a little, about $7k per day. N.Y.C. stays tight, so the spread is $80/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 80). P5 loses about $288k per day and P2 gains about $48k per day. Gas and spikes are unshocked. Net is roughly -$260k per day, or about -$6.5M over 25 days. The estimate is a linear extrapolation and uncertain.

A 30-day warm summer pattern has load only 3% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.03), while the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread stays $65/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 65) because of local constraints. WEST on-peak prices come in 15% below the load-implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -15) and real-time clears 15% below day-ahead (dart_pct -15), which trims P1 and P4. A $5/MMBtu delivered-gas premium (ny_gas_basis_usd 5) hits only the heat-rate call P4 by raising its fuel cost, costing about $20k per day. Henry Hub is unchanged. P5 loses about $230k per day and P2 gains about $39k. Net is roughly -$230k per day, or about -$6.9M over 30 days. I state a lower $6M because the linear extrapolation is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day summer heat pattern in which the load shock itself is negligible (load_peak_ratio 1.0, so no load-driven price rise helps the long WEST positions). The only shock is a persistent N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widening of $75/MWh on every day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 75), from import limits into the city and local unit constraints. The short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 loses about $3,200 per day for each $/MWh of widening, roughly $7.2M over 30 days. The long spread position P2 earns $600 per $/MWh per day, about $1.35M back. P1 and P4 stay flat because WEST is unshocked. Gas, DART and spikes are not shocked. Net is about -$5.8M. This is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A 30-day hot summer with daily peak load 10% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.1), which scales up the short N.Y.C. load obligation P5. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $55/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55) because of city constraints. Upstate is oversupplied, so WEST on-peak is 20% below the level the load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -20), which removes the usual heat-wave gain of the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. A $2/MMBtu delivered-gas premium (ny_gas_basis_usd 2) cuts the payoff of P4 only. P5 loses about $6.3M, P2 earns about $1.0M, and P1 and P4 together lose about $0.5M. Henry Hub, DART and spikes are not shocked. Net is about -$5.8M. The estimate extrapolates the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

A 30-day summer heat pattern with load 5% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.05) while Henry Hub falls 35% (gas_hh_pct -35) on weak gas demand and storage surplus, inside the historical summer range. Cheaper gas pulls WEST on-peak power down, which cuts the gain of the long swap P1 by about $0.6M. WEST also clears a further 10% below the implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -10), costing P1 and P4 about $0.5M in total. N.Y.C. stays tight and the spread is $55/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55). P5 loses about $6.0M and P2 gains about $1.0M. DART and spikes are not shocked. Net is about -$5.7M, and I state a slightly lower figure because the linear extrapolation is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day summer pattern with normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0), so no load-driven price rise helps the long WEST positions. Henry Hub falls 30% (gas_hh_pct -30), inside the historical summer minimum of -44.2%, and upstate is oversupplied, so WEST on-peak sits a further 15% below the implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -15). This cuts the value of the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. N.Y.C. stays constrained, so the spread is $50/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 50) on every day. Calibrating on earlier engine runs, P5 loses about $3,400 per day per $/MWh of widening, roughly $5.1M over 30 days. P2 earns back about $0.9M, and P1 and P4 lose about $1.3M together. Net is about -$5.5M. This is a linear extrapolation and uncertain.

A 25-day summer heat episode with normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0). Import limits into N.Y.C. widen the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $70/MWh on each day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70), within the historical summer maximum of 289.7. Upstate is oversupplied, so WEST on-peak is 20% below the implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -20), trimming the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. A $3/MMBtu delivered-gas premium (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) lowers the payoff of P4 only. Henry Hub and DART are not shocked and there are no spike days. Scaling earlier engine runs, P5 loses about $6.0M, P2 earns about $1.05M, and P1 and P4 lose about $0.85M together. Net is about -$5.8M. I state a slightly lower figure because the extrapolation is uncertain.

A 30-day summer pattern with normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) in which day-ahead over-forecasts the heat, so real-time clears 30% below day-ahead (dart_pct -30). This lowers the WEST price seen by the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, while the DART receipt P3 gains a little. Henry Hub is 25% lower (gas_hh_pct -25) on weak gas demand, and WEST on-peak is a further 10% below the implied level (ref_onpeak_pct -10). N.Y.C. stays tight, so the spread is $45/MWh wider (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45). P5 loses about $4.6M, P2 earns about $0.8M, P1 and P4 lose about $1.8M together, and P3 gains about $0.2M. Net is about -$5.4M. This is a linear extrapolation and uncertain.

scenario.narrative: Causal chain: a winter pipeline constraint into the downstate gas market pushes gas up, and N.Y.C. generators, which depend on gas and run on it at the margin, set prices. N.Y.C. prices detach from WEST, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens. gas_hh_pct = +60 is a Henry Hub rise, inside the winter historical range. ny_gas_basis_usd = +20 only lowers the P4 heat-rate payoff. pocket_minus_ref_usd = +150 for 15 days is the main driver: it hurts the 140 MW retail short in P5 far more than it helps the 25 MW long spread in P2. Load stays at normal (ratio 1.0), with no spikes, no DART shock and no extra WEST move. The WEST gains in P1 and P4 from the gas rise are small and offset only a fraction of the loss. My estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities linearly: spread loss about $6.9M, gas gains about $0.6M, so the net loss is about $6.3M. Nonlinearity could change this.

That hurts the long P1 swap and the P4 call, whose loss is capped near its base payoff. pocket_minus_ref_usd = +100 for 20 days widens the spread and drives most of the loss through the P5 retail short, partly offset by P2. Load stays at normal (ratio 1.0), with no spikes and no DART shock. The estimate scales the 5-day sensitivities linearly: spread loss about $6.2M, WEST decline about $0.6M, gas gains about $0.5M, so the net loss is about $6.0M. This is an approximation: the combined effects are not additive and the P4 cap is uncertain.

Causal chain: an acute winter gas curtailment in the downstate market, with Henry Hub +120% and ny_gas_basis_usd = +30, which lowers P4 only. N.Y.C. oil and gas units become marginal at very high cost, so pocket_minus_ref_usd = +300 for 8 days is a sharp but historically bounded widening, below the winter historical maximum of 400.6. load_peak_ratio = 1.10 reflects cold weather lifting N.Y.C. load, which scales up the P5 retail short. WEST rises with gas, so P1 and P4 gain, but these gains are small next to the spread loss. There are no spikes and no DART shock. Spread loss is about $8.3M after the load scaling, less about $0.9M of WEST gains, so the net loss is about $7.0M. This is a linear-scaling estimate, not an engine result.

TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: gas_supply
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):
{
 "active_positions": [
  "P1",
  "P2",
  "P3",
  "P4",
  "P5",
  "P6"
 ],
 "allocated_capital_usd": 20000000.0,
 "book": [
  {
   "channel": "system",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price is above K1",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak price is below K1",
   "position": "P1",
   "what": "Long 100 MW swap on the WEST on-peak price, strike K1 = 39.49 $/MWh, 16 h per on-peak weekday"
  },
  {
   "channel": "congestion",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens above c0",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",
   "what": "Long 25 MW of the N.Y.C. minus WEST price spread around the clock (24 h), strike c0 = 11.60 $/MWh"
  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",
   "what": "Retail load obligation: short 140 MW x (load / normal load) in N.Y.C. at fixed price R = 45.65, hedged by a long WEST position at H = 34.05, 24 h; P&L = (R - N.Y.C. price) + (WEST price - H), times load"
  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

That cuts the daily peak by about 5% (load_peak_ratio 0.95). This is the main loss driver: P5 loses about $15.9k per $/MWh per 5 days against a P2 gain of $3k, a net of about -$2.6k per $/MWh per day, or roughly -$7.0M over 30 days. scenario.narrative: Large-load arrivals fall about 900 MW short of the 2030 Gold Book path, so peak load is about 3% lower (load_peak_ratio 0.97). WEST is oversupplied and its on-peak price drops a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct -35), which cuts P1 and P4 gains. A $2/MWh N.Y.C.-only gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2) lowers the P4 heat-rate payoff further. N.Y.C. prices hold while WEST softens, and a transmission-limited pocket widens the spread by $110/MWh for 20 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 110). That is a net loss of about $2.6k per $/MWh per day on P5 less P2, or about -$5.7M. Lower WEST prices and load add about -$0.9M. Gas, DART and spike shocks are zero. The loss is a linear extrapolation from the 5-day sensitivities and ignores the basis effect, so it is conservative.

scenario.narrative: Large-load arrivals fall about 1,400 MW short of the 2035 Gold Book path, so peak load is about 6% lower (load_peak_ratio 0.94). Weak upstate demand pulls Henry Hub down 25% (gas_hh_pct -25) and WEST on-peak power falls a further 50% (ref_onpeak_pct -50). Both hurt the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. A $3/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) further reduces P4's payoff. For 14 days the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens sharply by $150/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 150), inside the historical maximum of 289.7. The short-N.Y.C. retail hedge P5 loses about $15.9k per $/MWh per 5 days against a P2 gain of $3k, so the spread alone costs about -$5.4M. Lower WEST prices, lower gas and lower load add about -$1.3M. This is a shorter, sharper event than the other two scenarios. The loss is a linear extrapolation from the 5-day sensitivities and is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

Upstate is oversupplied, so WEST on-peak falls a further 25% (ref_onpeak_pct -25). Day-ahead over-procured for load that never arrived, so real-time clears 45% below day-ahead (dart_pct -45), which lowers the WEST real-time settlement for the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. N.Y.C. stays import-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $45/MWh wider for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45). P5 loses about $4.4M and P2 gains about $0.8M. P1 loses about $1.8M and P4 about $0.8M, partly offset by a P3 gain of about $0.3M. Gas, basis and spike shocks are zero. This is a linear extrapolation from the 5-day sensitivities, so it is uncertain.

The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $55/MWh wider for 25 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 55), costing P5 about $4.5M against a P2 gain of about $0.8M. The P1 loss is about $1.5M and the P4 loss about $0.7M. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

The daily peak falls about 5% (load_peak_ratio 0.95). Upstate is oversupplied, so WEST on-peak falls a further 45% (ref_onpeak_pct -45) and Henry Hub falls 30% (gas_hh_pct -30). Slightly softer upstate demand lowers the WEST on-peak price a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15), which trims the long WEST positions P1 and P4. N.Y.C. stays constrained by its own generation and import limits, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $80/MWh wider for 25 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 80). A $3/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 3) cuts the P4 payoff more. The spread is only $30/MWh wider for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 30), so P5 loses about $2.8M against a P2 gain of about $0.55M. The loss is led by the system and gas channels: P1 loses about $3.3M and P4 about $1.1M, partly offset by a P3 gain of about $0.3M. This is a linear extrapolation, P4's loss is capped by its base payoff, and the estimate is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads arrive about 700 MW slower than the Gold Book path, toward the low end of the 2030 range (large_load_shock_mw -700). The daily peak is about 2% lower (load_peak_ratio 0.98). Upstate is mildly oversupplied, so WEST on-peak falls a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15), which trims the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. N.Y.C. stays import-constrained, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $60/MWh wider for all 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 60). That is the main driver. P5 loses about $5.8M and P2 gains about $1.1M. P1 loses about $0.65M and P4 about $0.3M. Gas, basis, DART and spike shocks are zero. This is a linear extrapolation from engine results on similar earlier scenarios, so it is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads arrive about 1,200 MW slower than the Gold Book path, between the 2030 and 2035 shortfall cases (large_load_shock_mw -1200). The daily peak is about 3% lower (load_peak_ratio 0.97). WEST is oversupplied, so its on-peak price falls a further 25% (ref_onpeak_pct -25). Real-time clears 20% below day-ahead (dart_pct -20) because day-ahead over-procured for load that never arrived. A $2/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2) lowers the P4 payoff to its capped loss. The spread is $50/MWh wider for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 50). Estimated P&L: P5 about -$4.7M, P2 about +$0.9M, P1 about -$1.2M, P4 about -$0.8M, P3 about +$0.15M. Gas and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: Large new loads arrive about 1,000 MW slower than the Gold Book path, close to the 2030 shortfall case (large_load_shock_mw -1000). The daily peak is about 4% lower (load_peak_ratio 0.96). Missing data-center gas burn pulls Henry Hub down 25% (gas_hh_pct -25) and WEST on-peak falls a further 40% (ref_onpeak_pct -40). Real-time clears 45% below day-ahead (dart_pct -45). These cut the long swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, and a $2/MMBtu N.Y.C. gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2) caps P4's loss. The spread is $42/MWh wider for 30 days (pocket_minus_ref_usd 42). Estimated P&L: P1 about -$2.3M, P4 about -$0.83M, P5 about -$3.9M, P2 about +$0.75M, P3 about +$0.2M. This is a system and gas led scenario and the estimate is uncertain.
